definition: Finds objects, people, text, scenes, and unsafe content in images and videos, and performs face analysis and face search. Think: computer vision as a service.
Converts speech to text automatically, for example subtitles or call transcripts. It can also redact personal information and handle multiple languages.
The opposite of Transcribe: turns text into lifelike speech, so applications can talk. Great for audio versions of articles and voice prompts.
Natural language processing service. Reads text to find sentiment, key phrases, entities, language, and topics, for example analyzing customer reviews or emails.
Fully managed service for data scientists and developers to build, train, and deploy their own custom machine learning models.
Builds real-time personalized product recommendations using the same technology as Amazon.com, with no machine learning expertise needed.
You rent the building blocks: servers, networking, and storage, and you manage the operating system and software. Example: Amazon EC2.
The provider manages servers and operating systems; you just deploy your application code and data. Example: AWS Elastic Beanstalk.
A complete application that the provider runs and manages; you simply sign in and use it. Examples: Gmail, Dropbox, and Zoom.
A separate geographic area, such as Frankfurt or Tokyo, made of multiple Availability Zones. Choose one by compliance, latency, service availability, and price.
One or more discrete data centers with redundant power and networking, isolated from other zones in the same Region but linked by low-latency connections.
Scale up: make one instance bigger, for example from a large to an extra large instance type. Common for databases, but it has a hardware limit.
Scale out: add more instances to share the load, and scale in by removing them. This is what Auto Scaling Groups do for distributed systems.
Layer 7 load balancer for HTTP and HTTPS traffic. Can route requests by URL path or host name to different target groups.
Layer 4 load balancer for TCP and UDP traffic. Handles millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency and supports static IP addresses.
AWS best-practice guide built on six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, and sustainability.
AWS guidance for digital transformation, organized into six perspectives: business, people, governance, platform, security, and operations.
Free community question and answer site for AWS that replaced the old AWS Forums. Community experts and AWS staff answer technical questions.
Shows the estimated carbon emissions from your AWS usage and how they change over time. Supports the sustainability pillar.
Collects, processes, and analyzes streaming data in real time, such as clickstreams, application logs, and IoT sensor readings.
Managed message broker for RabbitMQ and ActiveMQ. Use it when migrating on-premises apps that rely on open protocols like AMQP or MQTT.
Placing a queue, topic, or stream between application parts so each can scale or fail independently. Examples: SQS queues, SNS topics, and Kinesis streams.
Cloud Development Kit: define infrastructure in familiar programming languages like Python or TypeScript. The code is converted into a CloudFormation template.
Opens a secure shell on EC2 and on-premises servers without SSH keys, a bastion host, or an open port 22. Sessions can be logged.
Secure, serverless storage for configuration values and secrets, such as database connection strings, optionally encrypted with KMS and versioned.
Security Token Service: issues temporary, limited-privilege credentials, for example when a user or service assumes an IAM role.
Identity for your web and mobile app users. Handles sign-up and sign-in for millions of users, including login with Google or Facebook.
Runs Microsoft Active Directory on AWS. Options: AWS Managed Microsoft AD, AD Connector to proxy to on-premises AD, and Simple AD.
Extensions of a Region placed in large metro areas, bringing compute, storage, and databases closer to users for single-digit millisecond latency.
AWS infrastructure embedded inside telecom 5G networks, giving mobile devices ultra-low latency. Think: connected cars, live video, and augmented reality.
CloudWatch Metrics track numbers over time, like CPU utilization. Alarms watch a metric and notify through SNS or trigger actions like Auto Scaling.
Collects, stores, and searches log files from applications, Lambda, EC2 with the CloudWatch agent, and on-premises servers. Retention is configurable.
Traces requests as they travel through distributed applications, showing a service map, so you can find bottlenecks and errors.
Continuously replicates physical, virtual, and cloud servers into AWS, so you can recover them quickly, within minutes, after a disaster.
Runs controlled chaos engineering experiments, like stopping instances or adding CPU stress, to test how resilient a workload really is.
